title: Marriage, Children, Wealth, and the Ransom for Many
summary: On the road south toward Jerusalem Jesus answers a question about divorce by pointing back to creation, blesses little children, and tells a rich man who has kept the commandments to sell everything and follow him. He predicts his death a third time, and when James and John ask for places of honor he teaches that greatness means service, because the Son of Man came to serve and give his life as a ransom for many. At Jericho he restores the sight of blind Bartimaeus, who follows him on the road.
story: Jesus has now left Galilee for good. The chapter follows him through Perea, east of the Jordan, and then to Jericho, the last town before the climb to Jerusalem. It completes the central section of Mark (8:27 to 10:52), which began with a partly blind man healed in two stages and ends with a blind man who sees clearly and follows Jesus on the road. Between those two healings Jesus has predicted his death three times, and each time the disciples have misunderstood. Here the misunderstanding is at its sharpest: right after the most detailed prediction of all, two of the inner circle ask for thrones. Jesus' answer, verse 45, gives the meaning of everything that is about to happen in Jerusalem.
historical:
Perea, the region beyond the Jordan, was part of the territory of Herod Antipas, the ruler who had executed John the Baptist for condemning his marriage to his brother's wife. A question about divorce asked in Antipas's land was not idle; it could draw Jesus into the same danger. The Pharisees' question also reflects a live debate among Jewish teachers. Deuteronomy 24:1 allowed a man to divorce his wife for some indecency and required him to give her a written certificate. The school of Shammai read that as sexual immorality; the school of Hillel read it broadly enough to cover almost any displeasure. The certificate itself protected the woman, since it proved she was free to remarry.

Jericho, an oasis city near the Jordan about fifteen miles northeast of Jerusalem, had been rebuilt by Herod the Great, who kept a winter palace there. Pilgrims from Galilee often traveled south along the Jordan to avoid Samaria and then climbed the steep road from Jericho up to Jerusalem, a rise of more than three thousand feet. The crowd around Jesus was likely made up partly of pilgrims going up for Passover. The prediction that the Son of Man would be delivered to the Gentiles points to Roman involvement, since only the Roman governor could order an execution.
cultural:
In Jewish law a husband could divorce his wife, but a wife generally could not divorce her husband. Roman law allowed either spouse to end a marriage, and Herodias herself had left her first husband, so Jesus' words in verse 12 addressed a world where both happened. Children in the ancient world were loved but had no standing; they could not repay anyone or advance anyone's cause, which is why the disciples thought them a distraction. Wealth was widely taken as a sign of God's blessing, so the disciples' amazement in verses 24 and 26 is genuine: if the rich cannot be saved, who can?

The camel and the needle's eye are a deliberate impossibility, the largest animal in the region and the smallest opening. The suggestion that the needle was a small gate in Jerusalem's wall has no ancient evidence behind it. Sitting at a king's right and left meant the highest positions of honor. In the Old Testament the cup is a common image for the portion God pours out, often his judgment (Psalm 75:8, Isaiah 51:17), and baptism here means being plunged or overwhelmed. A ransom was the price paid to free a slave or a prisoner of war, or to redeem a life that was forfeit. Bartimaeus's cloak was likely spread on the ground to collect alms, and throwing it off meant leaving his livelihood behind.
literary: The chapter is built from encounters on the road, each of which turns a common value upside down. Marriage is judged by creation rather than by what the law permits; children, not adults, model how to receive the kingdom; a rich and righteous man is told he lacks one thing; the first will be last. Verses 32 to 34 give the fullest of the three passion predictions, with seven verbs (delivered, condemn, deliver, mock, spit, flog, kill) and a promise of resurrection, and verses 35 to 45 give the fullest misunderstanding and the fullest explanation. Jesus asks James and John and then Bartimaeus the same question, “What do you want Me to do for you?” (verses 36 and 51). The two answers show the contrast Mark wants readers to see: disciples asking for glory, a beggar asking for sight. Mark's last sentence about Bartimaeus places him as a model disciple: he followed Jesus along the road.

outline.t: Divorce and God's intent in creation
The rich man who went away sad
Wealth, the kingdom, and the reward of those who leave all
James and John ask for glory: the Son of Man came to serve

doctrines.note: Verse 45 is Mark's clearest statement of why Jesus came: to give his life as a ransom for many. His death is a price paid to set others free, given in their place. The word many echoes Isaiah 53:11-12, where the servant bears the sin of many.

Jesus grounds marriage in creation, quoting Genesis 1:27 and 2:24: God made them male and female, and the two become one flesh. Moses' provision for divorce was a concession to hardness of heart, not God's design. Jesus also honors children as the models of how the kingdom is received.

The rich man asks what he must do, and the disciples ask who can be saved. Jesus' answer is that salvation is impossible for human beings and possible for God. It is received like a child receives a gift, not earned like an inheritance secured by performance.
In the kingdom, greatness is service and the first are last. Jesus contrasts the rulers of the Gentiles, who lord it over others, with his own way, and he defines that way by his own death.

words.note: Lutron, ransom, the price paid to release a slave or captive. In the Greek Old Testament related words describe redeeming a firstborn son or buying back property or a person. Jesus uses it of his own life given for many, and the phrase is the seed of the New Testament's teaching that Christ's death was a costly act of liberation, given in the place of others.

Diakoneo, to serve, originally to wait at table. It is what Peter's mother-in-law did when healed (1:31) and what the women who followed Jesus did (15:41). The Son of Man, the figure who in Daniel 7 is served by all peoples, reverses the picture: he came not to be served but to serve.

Sklerokardia, hardness of heart, a compound of hard and heart. The Greek Old Testament uses it of Israel's stubbornness (Deuteronomy 10:16). Jesus says Moses' divorce regulation was written because of it, a provision for a broken situation, not a statement of God's original will.

Apoluo, to release or send away, the ordinary word for divorce in this context. It is the same verb used for dismissing a crowd (6:45). The Pharisees ask whether a man may send his wife away; Jesus answers by asking what God joined.

christ: This chapter shows who Jesus is by showing why he came. He is the Son of Man who goes up to Jerusalem knowing he will be handed over, mocked, flogged, and killed, and who will rise after three days. He goes ahead of his disciples on the road (verse 32), leading them toward his own death. He is the servant who gives his life as a ransom, the fulfillment of Isaiah's suffering servant who bears the sin of many. And he is the Son of David, the title Bartimaeus shouts at Jericho, the first time anyone uses it of Jesus in Mark, just before Jesus enters David's city. The king who is about to be acclaimed in Jerusalem will reign by serving, and the cup he drinks is the one his disciples could not yet understand.

hard.q: Does Jesus' teaching on divorce mean that divorce and remarriage are never permitted?
hard.a: Jesus' words in Mark are the most absolute form of his teaching. Matthew's parallels include an exception for sexual immorality (Matthew 5:32 and 19:9), and Paul adds that a believer deserted by an unbelieving spouse is not bound (1 Corinthians 7:15). Christians have read these texts in different ways. Some hold that marriage cannot be dissolved except by death, and that remarriage after divorce is not permitted while a former spouse lives; this view has deep roots in the Western church. Many Protestants hold that adultery and desertion are legitimate grounds for divorce and that the innocent party may remarry. Others add abuse and other grave betrayals as forms of breaking the marriage covenant. What all these views share is Jesus' main point: God designed marriage as a lifelong union, and divorce is always a tearing of what he joined, not a neutral legal option. Readers carrying the pain of a broken marriage should also hear that Jesus spoke these words to men who were using the law to dismiss wives freely, and that his words protected the vulnerable. This note is not legal advice; anyone facing separation or abuse should seek help from their church and from qualified professionals.

questions: Jesus looked at the rich man and loved him before asking him to give everything up. What might be the one thing you lack, the thing that holds you back from following him fully?
What does it mean for you to receive the kingdom like a child, and what adult habits make that hard?
James and John asked for glory; Bartimaeus asked for sight. If Jesus asked you, “What do you want Me to do for you?” what would you honestly say?
